Social media launch plan

Make the machine feel like the easiest healthy choice in London.

The food has to look generous. The machine has to look convenient. The brand has to feel modern, fresh and useful.

The social idea

Do not sell “salad”. Sell a proper protein lunch that happens to be ready in 30 seconds.

Food first

Big protein portions, bright ingredients, sauce pours, crunch and freshness.

Healthy but filling

Show meals people actually want after a commute or before the gym. Never make it feel like diet food.

The machine is content

Restocking, tapping to pay, choosing a bowl, low stock and sold out moments are naturally watchable.

Example food and vending imagery used for planning purposes. Final launch photography should feature your own bowls and machine.

Who we are speaking to

Waterloo, Victoria and other high-footfall stations: hungry people, very little time.

Morning and lunch commuters

People rushing between train, office and meetings who want something better than another sandwich.

No queueReady nowHigh protein

Gym and after-work crowd

People who want a convenient high-protein meal on the way to training or on the journey home.

FreshFillingEasy macros

What we post

1. Food that makes people hungry

Close ups of the bowls, the protein, the dressing going on and the first forkful. Keep videos short and bright.

2. The 30 second lunch

Film the whole journey from approaching the machine to walking away with lunch. This is the clearest reason to choose us.

3. Building the business

Show taste tests, packaging choices, site hunting, mistakes, first deliveries and first sales. Real beats polished.

4. Customers choosing for us

Ask which bowl, protein or dip should stay. People are more likely to try something they helped choose.

Launch plan

4 weeks out
Start the story. “We are building a protein salad vending brand for London commuters.” Show the logo, machine concept and food tests.
2 weeks out
Let people vote. Bowl vs bowl. Dip vs dip. Ask “Which one would you grab at Waterloo?” Start collecting followers before opening.
Launch week
Make the machine the event. First restock, first customer, first 50 sales, best seller, what sold out first and real reactions.
After launch
Turn buyers into content. Tag us with your bowl, weekly free lunch draw, customer reviews and “today’s top seller”.

First month content

Week 1

Why London lunch needs a better option. Founder story. Station lunch rush. What we are building.

Week 2

Food week. Show the 8 bowls, protein amounts, sauces, taste tests and customer voting.

Week 3

Machine week. How it works, payment, refrigeration, restocking and “lunch in 30 seconds”.

Week 4

Launch countdown. Free lunch giveaway, exact location reveal, first-day offer and launch-day filming.

Videos worth making

“Would you buy this at Waterloo?”

Three bowls. Fast close ups. Ask people to choose in comments.

“What £7 gets you”

Open the box, show the protein and dressing, then show the empty bowl afterwards.

“Restocking at 11:30am”

Satisfying rows of fresh bowls going into the machine just before lunch.

“Which dip wins?”

Five dips, one bowl, quick taste reactions. Let customers decide what stays.

“Day one: what actually sold?”

Share the real numbers. People follow journeys, not adverts.

“Lunch before your train leaves”

Put a timer on screen from purchase to walking back towards the platform.

The rule

Every post should make someone think one of three things: that looks good, that looks easy, or I want to try that.

5xstrong posts a week is enough to start

Simple weekly rhythm

Monday

Founder or business update.

Tuesday

Food close up or bowl reveal.

Wednesday

Commuter or station video.

Thursday

Taste test, dip test or customer vote.

Friday

Machine restock, sales update or customer reactions.

Stories

Post naturally throughout the week: stock levels, polls, behind the scenes and quick updates.

Keep it natural

Do

Use phones, real customers, real food, short captions, honest numbers and London locations people recognise.

Avoid

Long educational posts, fake health claims, gym-bro language, over-produced adverts and generic stock content once you launch.
